To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the flow into ischemic tissue and across the collaterals is regulated by separate waterfalls.
the pressure-flow relationship in an ischemic bed has a back pressure-independent component that is due to a waterfall phenomenon on coronary collateral vessels.

the pressure-flow relationships for flow into ischemic tissue are consistent with the presence of a waterfall mechanism on collateral vessels and that a waterfall mechanism also operates on the vessels within the ischemic tissue.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanism(s) responsible for the flow limitation in ischemic myocardial beds.
the flow of blood into ischemic myocardial tissue.
the flow characteristics in the ischemic bed.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
flow into ischemic tissue is regulated by a waterfall mechanism on the collateral vessels and a waterfall mechanism on vessels within the ischemic tissue.
a waterfall mechanism operates on the collaterers, and that this mechanism operates at a back pressure of approximately 20 mmHg.
a waterfall mechanism exists in the ischemic bed and that the waterfall pressure is about 10 mmHg, whereas in collateral vessels it is about 20 mmHg.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the pressure-flow relationship in ischemic myocardial tissue can be described as the sum of the flow through a waterfall mechanism on collateral vessels (back pressure-independent flow) and the flow through a pressure-dependent mechanism in the ischemic tissue.
the flow into ischemic tissue is modulated by a waterfall phenomenon that operates on both the collateral vessels and the vessels in the tissue.
a waterfall phenomenon exists on the collateral vessels and on vessels within the ischemic bed.
The main takeaway from our work is that
extravascular pressures in the heart can exceed 20 mm HG.
the pressure-flow relationship in the ischemic bed is back pressure-independent below a critical pressure of approximately 10 mm Hgs.
the pressure-flow relationship in ischemic myocardial is not linear, as is commonly assumed in mathematical modeling of myocardial perfusion.
